analysis.one_liner: Ends taxpayer-subsidized old-growth logging contracts in Alaska's Tongass forest and temporarily protects about 1.8 million acres of rain forest.
analysis.headline: The Tongass reform bill drew 53 Senate cosponsors and three rounds of hearings, but never reached a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal parts of the Alaska lands law that guarantee federal money to keep timber flowing to two pulp companies, terminate their long-term timber sale contracts, and require a rewrite of the Tongass forest management plan that puts fish, wildlife, subsistence, and recreation on equal footing with logging. It would also halt logging and road building on roughly 1.8 million acres of particularly valuable old-growth habitat until the new plan is finished [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Southeast Alaska's commercial fishing, recreation, and tourism industries and subsistence users, whose economy depends on fish, wildlife, and old-growth habitat the bill protects [S3]. Taxpayers also gain: the bill repeals the law requiring annual appropriations to maintain a timber supply for two private pulp companies and requires an accounting of what the timber sale program actually costs and earns [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fishermen, tourism operators, subsistence users, taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that Congress appropriate money each year to maintain a timber supply from the Tongass for dependent private industry, ending a standing federal subsidy.
Terminates within 90 days the long-term timber sale contracts between the United States and Alaska Pulp Corporation and between the United States and Ketchikan Pulp Company.

Requires a full revision of the 1979 Tongass forest plan to significantly increase protection of fish, wildlife, watershed, old-growth, and subsistence resources, which the bill identifies as the foundation of the commercial fishing, recreation, and tourism economy of southeast Alaska.

Bars timber sales, harvesting, and road construction on about 1.8 million acres across 23 named areas of high value for fish, wildlife, subsistence, and recreation until the revised plan takes effect.

Expands the annual report to Congress to cover timber harvest effects on wildlife, fisheries, recreation, biological diversity, and the old-growth rain forest, plus timber supply and demand and the costs and revenues of the timber sale program.

analysis.who_pays: Alaska Pulp Corporation and Ketchikan Pulp Company would lose their long-term contracts for below-cost federal timber, and the logging-dependent economy around those mills would bear the adjustment. Taxpayers would stop paying, since the bill repeals the requirement for appropriations to maintain the timber supply for industry [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Alaska pulp mills and logging towns

drawbacks.text: Terminating the pulp mills' long-term contracts within 90 days, with no transition program in the bill, would put mill jobs in towns like Ketchikan and Sitka at immediate risk and hit logging-dependent workers and communities hardest.

The logging and road-building moratorium on about 1.8 million acres would cut timber deliveries during the plan revision, tightening supply for the remaining industry and for workers before any replacement economy matures.

An honest supporter would concede the bill gave no offsetting economic plan for southeast Alaska mill towns that had been promised timber under federal law since 1980; protection of fish and old growth would arrive first, alternative jobs later, if at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: ending a standing federal subsidy to two private pulp companies, protecting fish and old-growth habitat that anchor the region's fishing and tourism economy, and forcing the first honest accounting of what the timber sale program costs versus earns. The costs are real but concentrated: mill jobs and logging work in a handful of southeast Alaska towns would be jeopardized quickly, and the bill offered them no transition plan, which is the strongest objection to it and likely a reason it stalled even with a Senate majority behind it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee through three rounds of hearings and an unfavorable review from the Department of Agriculture, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 1989, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, then to its Public Lands subcommittee.
The subcommittee held hearings in Washington in February 1989 and field hearings in Ketchikan and Sitka, Alaska in April 1989, and again in February 1990.
In April 1989 the committee received an unfavorable executive comment from the Department of Agriculture, the agency that runs the Forest Service.
The bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pulp mills kept their long-term contracts and the guaranteed federal timber supply arrangements stayed in place, since the bill never advanced. Southeast Alaska's fishing, tourism, and subsistence interests saw no new protections from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pulp mills and the Forest Service

for.name: Sen. Timothy Wirth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 53 cosponsors, including Republicans, to end subsidized old-growth logging contracts in the Tongass

for.name: Senate cosponsors
for.role: 53 cosponsors (43 of 55 Senate Democrats, 10 of 45 Senate Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 43 Democrats and 10 Republicans, a majority of the Senate

for.name: Senate Energy subcommittee leadership holding Alaska field hearings
for.role: Subcommittee on Public Lands, National Parks
for.what_they_did: Held hearings in Washington and on location in Ketchikan and Sitka, Alaska, on the bill

against.what_they_did: Submitted an unfavorable executive comment on the bill to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, with 43 of 55 Senate Democrats and 10 of 45 Senate Republicans cosigning; the visible resistance in the record came from the Department of Agriculture's unfavorable comment rather than a party bloc [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Alaska pulp and timber mills (Alaska Pulp Corporation, Ketchikan Pulp Company)
industries.note: The bill would terminate the companies' long-term federal timber contracts within 90 days and repeal the guaranteed appropriations that kept timber flowing to them below cost. Their gain in the existing arrangement came from harvesting public old-growth timber on terms the bill called unsustainable for fish, wildlife, and the broader economy.

industries.industry: Logging and road construction contractors in southeast Alaska
industries.note: Logging and road-building contractors would lose work during the moratorium on roughly 1.8 million acres and face a smaller long-term timber supply under the revised forest plan.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing, recreation, and tourism in southeast Alaska
industries.note: The bill would require the forest plan to protect the fish, wildlife, and scenic resources these industries and subsistence users depend on, and names the commercial fishing industry as a consulted party.
